blocks.text: 1. Customer Support Bot
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785448061583-862100015.png

Enterprise Search closed by pointing toward chat with PDFs for one user's own documents instead. Customer Support Bot, a RAG system design for automated, grounded customer assistance, turns the retrieval and generation techniques covered throughout this course toward a public-facing, high-stakes use case.
It answers customer questions from a support knowledge base while escalating what it cannot resolve.
2. The Design Problem's Scope
Unlike Enterprise Search's internal employees, this system faces external customers directly.
Every answer represents the company, raising the stakes of an ungrounded or wrong response.

blocks.content: {"headers":["System","Audience"],"rows":[["Enterprise search","Internal employees"],["Customer support bot","External customers, representing the company"]]}

blocks.text: 3. Grounding In A Curated Support Knowledge Base

Building on the practice of breaking the answer into individual claims covered in Faithfulness, the knowledge base here is deliberately curated support articles and FAQs, not the entire company's raw documents.
A narrower, cleaner source makes faithfulness easier to guarantee.
4. System Prompting For Tone And Boundaries

blocks.alt: System Prompting For Tone And Boundaries
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785448061584-874549882.png
Setting the model's role, tone, and boundaries, as covered in System Prompting, matters more here: a support bot needs an explicitly friendly, on-brand tone distinct from a generic assistant.
The system prompt also draws the boundary of what topics the bot will and will not address.
5. Escalating To A Human When Confidence Is Low

blocks.alt: Escalating To A Human When Confidence Is Low
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785448061584-489611327.png
As Hit Rate covers, a low hit rate means the retrieval step is failing outright, and a query with no good retrieved match signals the bot cannot actually help.
Escalating to a human agent beats forcing an unconfident, potentially wrong answer.

blocks.title: Note
blocks.content: A query returning no relevant chunk from the support knowledge base should trigger escalation to a human agent rather than the bot attempting a guess, the same low-hit-rate signal covered in Hit Rate.

blocks.text: 6. Using Conversation History For Troubleshooting Flows

blocks.alt: Using Conversation History For Troubleshooting Flows
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785448061584-597729711.png
Short-term memory within one conversation, covered in Memory, matters here because troubleshooting a problem often takes several back and forth turns, not one single question.
The bot must track what has already been tried before suggesting the next step.
7. Guardrails Against Off-Brand Or Offensive Responses

blocks.alt: Guardrails Against Off-Brand Or Offensive Responses
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785448061584-496946646.png
Layering guardrails at multiple points, as covered in Guardrails, is essential here: a public-facing bot needs both prompt level and output level checks against off-brand or inappropriate responses.
A single layer of protection is not enough for a system representing the company publicly.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Guardrail layer","What it checks"],"rows":[["Prompt level","Instructs tone, scope, and boundaries upfront"],["Output level","Independently verifies the response before it reaches the customer"]]}

blocks.text: 8. Measuring Support Bot Success With Real Metrics

blocks.alt: Measuring Support Bot Success With Real Metrics
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785448061584-448702643.png

Faithfulness and answer relevancy together cover both sides of answer quality, as established in Answer Relevancy, but a support bot's success is measured by resolution rate and escalation rate, not just answer quality alone.
Business metrics sit alongside the RAG quality metrics covered earlier.
9. Recognizing When This Customer Support Bot Design Fits The Actual Need

blocks.alt: Recognizing When This Customer Support Bot Design Fits The Actual Need
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785448061584-135088943.png
A company with a defined, curated support knowledge base fits this design.
Open-ended research across a huge, uncurated corpus fits enterprise search or a research assistant better instead.
10. Worked Example
The example below directly demonstrates escalation on low confidence and multi-turn troubleshooting using conversation history.

code.content:
support_articles = [
    {"id": "a1", "text": "To reset your password, click Forgot Password on the login page."},
    {"id": "a2", "text": "Refunds are processed within five business days of the request."},
]

def retrieve(query):
    return [a for a in support_articles if any(w in a["text"].lower() for w in query.lower().split())]

def support_bot_respond(query, conversation_history):
    # escalate when no matching article is found
    matches = retrieve(query)
    if not matches:
        return "I'm not confident I can resolve this. Let me connect you with a human agent.", conversation_history

    # track conversation history for troubleshooting continuity
    conversation_history.append({"query": query, "matched_article": matches[0]["id"]})
    return matches[0]["text"], conversation_history

history = []
response, history = support_bot_respond("How do I reset my password?", history)
print(f"Turn 1: {response}")

response, history = support_bot_respond("What about international shipping rates?", history)
print(f"Turn 2 (no match, should escalate): {response}")

print(f"\nConversation history so far: {history}")

blocks.title: Note
blocks.content: Running this example shows the password reset question answered directly while the shipping question with no matching article triggers escalation instead of a guessed answer.

blocks.text: 11. Common Mistakes

items: Grounding the bot in the entire company knowledge base instead of a curated support source.
Forcing an answer when retrieval finds no good match instead of escalating to a human.
Losing track of earlier troubleshooting steps across a multi-turn conversation.
Relying on a single guardrail layer for a system that represents the company publicly.

blocks.text: 12. Key Takeaways

items: A customer support bot answers questions from a support knowledge base and escalates what it cannot resolve.
Facing external customers directly raises the stakes of an ungrounded or wrong response.
Grounding in curated support articles rather than raw company documents makes faithfulness easier.
The system prompt sets an on-brand tone and draws the boundary of topics the bot will address.
A query with no good retrieved match should trigger escalation rather than a forced answer.
Multi-turn troubleshooting requires tracking what has already been tried in the conversation.
A public-facing bot needs both prompt level and output level guardrails, not just one layer.
Success is measured by resolution and escalation rate, not just RAG answer quality alone.
